G7A01: A bleeder resistor drains the filter capacitors after power is off, so they can't shock you.
G7A02: A power supply filter uses capacitors and inductors to smooth the pulses into steady DC.
G7A03: Two diodes with a center-tapped transformer = full-wave. A bridge uses four diodes and no center tap.
G7A04: A half-wave rectifier needs only one diode.
G7A05: Half-wave passes only one half of each cycle: 180 degrees.
G7A06: Full-wave uses both halves of the cycle: all 360 degrees.
G7A07: Full-wave flips every negative half up, so you get DC pulses at twice the AC frequency.
G7A08: A switchmode supply runs at high frequency, so its transformer and filter parts can be much smaller.
G7A09: Symbol 1 is the FET: a straight channel line with the gate on one side.
G7A10: Symbol 5 is the Zener diode: a diode whose bar has bent ends.
G7A11: Symbol 2 is the NPN transistor: the emitter arrow points out (Not Pointing iN).
G7A12: Symbol 6 is the solid core transformer: two coils with straight lines between them for the iron core.
G7A13: Symbol 7 is the tapped inductor: one coil with a connection coming off its middle.
G7B01: Neutralizing cancels the feedback that makes an amplifier oscillate on its own.
G7B02: Class C conducts for the smallest part of each cycle, so it wastes the least power: highest efficiency.
G7B03: AND: the output is high only when both inputs are high.
G7B04: Class A conducts the whole cycle: 100% of the time.
G7B05: Each bit has 2 states, so 3 bits = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 states.
G7B06: A shift register moves data one step along a row of circuits on each clock pulse.
G7B07: An oscillator is an amplifier with a filter feeding part of its output back to its input.
G7B08: Efficiency = RF power out divided by DC power in.
G7B09: An LC oscillator's frequency is set by the inductance and capacitance of its tank circuit.
G7B10: Linear = the output is a faithful, bigger copy of the input waveform.
G7B11: FM keeps a constant amplitude, so a non-linear Class C stage can amplify it. SSB and AM need linear amps.
G7C01: The balanced modulator makes both sidebands; a filter picks the one you want.
G7C02: A balanced modulator outputs double-sideband RF with the carrier suppressed.
G7C03: A matching transformer makes the transmitter and the feed line see the impedance they want.
G7C04: A product detector recovers the audio from a single sideband signal in the receiver.
G7C05: A DDS tunes over a wide range digitally while keeping crystal-oscillator stability.
G7C06: DSP filters are software, so you can create almost any bandwidth and shape.
G7C07: Insertion loss is how much a filter attenuates signals inside its passband.
G7C08: Front-end gain, demodulator bandwidth and front-end noise figure all affect sensitivity. All of these.
G7C09: I and Q are the same signal 90 degrees apart (in phase and quadrature).
G7C10: With I and Q, software can create or decode any type of modulation.
G7C11: In an SDR, software does filtering, detection and modulation. All of these.
G7C12: Cutoff frequency: where output falls to half power (3 dB down).
G7C13: Ultimate rejection is the best a filter can reject signals outside its passband.
G7C14: Bandwidth is measured between the upper and lower half-power (3 dB) points.
G8A01: Direct FSK changes the oscillator's frequency directly with the digital signal.
G8A02: Changing the phase angle to carry information is phase modulation.
G8A03: Changing the instantaneous frequency to carry information is frequency modulation.
G8A04: A reactance modulator on an amplifier stage shifts the phase, so the result is phase modulation.
G8A05: Amplitude modulation varies the instantaneous power level of the RF.
G8A06: QPSK31 is sideband sensitive, has error correction, and uses about the same bandwidth as BPSK31. All of these.
G8A07: Single sideband sends just one sideband with no carrier, so it is the narrowest phone mode.
G8A08: Overmodulation distorts the signal and spreads it out: excessive bandwidth (splatter).
G8A10: Flat-topping is the peaks clipped flat by too much drive or speech level.
G8A11: The modulation envelope is the outline you get by connecting the peaks of the modulated RF.
G8A12: QPSK sends two bits at a time using four phases: 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees.
G8A13: Link budget = transmit power plus antenna gains minus all losses, as seen at the receiver.
G8A14: Link margin = received power minus the minimum signal the receiver needs.
G8B01: You tune the local oscillator so each received signal mixes down to the same IF.
G8B02: An image is a signal twice the IF away from the one you want; it mixes to the same IF.
G8B03: Mixing two RF signals is heterodyning.
G8B04: A multiplier stage makes a harmonic to reach the final frequency in a VHF FM transmitter.
G8B05: Odd-order products (like 2F1 - F2) land right next to the original signals.
G8B06: Carson's rule: 2 x (deviation + audio) = 2 x (5 + 3) = 16 kHz.
G8B07: Multiplication: 146.52 / 12.21 = 12. Deviation is multiplied too, so the oscillator needs 5 kHz / 12 = 416.7 Hz.
G8B08: High duty cycle modes (FM, RTTY, FT8) can run the transmitter over its average power rating.
G8B09: Matching receiver bandwidth to the mode lets in the signal but as little noise as possible: best signal-to-noise ratio.
G8B10: Faster symbol rates need wider bandwidth.
G8B11: A mixer outputs the sum and the difference of its two input frequencies.
G8B12: Intermodulation: two signals mixing in a non-linear circuit to make unwanted outputs.
G8B13: Odd-order = the multipliers add to an odd number. 2F1 - F2: 2 + 1 = 3, odd.
G8C02: WSPR is a very low power beacon mode for checking HF propagation.
G8C03: A packet's header carries the routing and handling information.
G8C04: Baudot is a 5-bit code with start and stop bits added (used for RTTY).
G8C05: NAK = not acknowledged: please send that packet again.
G8C06: After too many failed tries, ARQ gives up and drops the connection.
G8C07: FT8 decodes signals far below the noise, at very low signal-to-noise ratios.
G8C08: Varicode gives common lowercase letters short codes, so uppercase letters take longer to send.
G8C09: In a mesh, if one node fails, packets can route through another node.
G8C10: FEC sends extra redundant data, so the receiver can rebuild what was lost.
G8C11: The two FSK frequencies are called mark and space.
G8C13: Vertical lines either side of a data signal on a waterfall mean overmodulation (splatter).
G8C14: Waterfall: frequency across, time running down, signal strength as brightness or color.
G8C15: FT8 reports are signal-to-noise in a 2.5 kHz bandwidth: +3 means 3 dB above the noise.
G8C16: DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion are the digital voice modes.
